item.title: Whose Peace Are You Keeping?
item.description:
People-Pleasing

Whose Peace Are You Keeping?

Redefining what “works” for the people-pleaser.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • People-pleasing in adulthood is correlated with relational trauma in childhood.
  • Prioritizing love from others over self-love is an outdated survival response.
  • Authenticity can foster healthy interpersonal relationships that don't depend on people-pleasing.
Source: bernardbodo / iStock

If you’ve ever caught yourself agreeing with someone to “keep the peace”, one of two things is likely happening: 1) you cannot be bothered to challenge this person since you don’t have a relationship with them, or, 2) you care so deeply about this individual liking you that you’re willing to sacrifice your authentic beliefs to validate them. The former is indifference and the latter is a fawn response; also known as people-pleasing.

Why do we people-please? The short answer is that, at some point in time, maintaining others’ peace was more important than our own.

What Worked Then

Consider a child raised in a high-conflict household; if someone ever disagreed with mom or dad, there would be severe consequences. What might that child have learned to survive in their environment? Agree with everyone to avoid being rejected. Let’s say the child sees how this mantra tends to keep the peace with mom and dad. As a bonus, they also gain a sense of control over their environment, which feels less scary than the truth; they ultimately cannot control mom or dad’s behaviour.

Source: Yuliia Kaveshnikova / iStock

At this point in their life, the child’s survival skills are genuinely protecting them from harm and neglect. In their experience, and in their defence, people-pleasing “works” because other people aren't upset with them and therefore, they are safe.

It makes sense that people-pleasing in adulthood is correlated with relational trauma in childhood; trauma whereby there was emotional and/or physical harm by any individual this child had a close relationship with. We’ll also find adults struggling with people-pleasing who operate on the narrative that the safety, or even maintenance, of a relationship relies on their ability to appease the other person. Through this lens, people-pleasing equals relationships, and authenticity equals isolation.

Why It Doesn’t Work Now

While it’s easy to pass self-judgment when reflecting on your pattern of fawning, what I’ve found is that it’s much harder to judge a child version of you—one who, in fact, appeased to protect you—than it is to judge your adult self. This is even an opportunity to thank this younger part of you for all their hard work, while also updating them on why it’s safe to be the real you now.

Source: Dilok Klaisataporn / iStock

Here’s the key difference between survival skills then and survival skills now: as a child, you were reliant on your parents for basic needs being met. The thought of them not loving you or hurting you would be too overwhelming to bear, and so you took it into your own hands to try and make sure that didn’t happen. This pattern is most often subconscious for the child but can be consciously reversed in adulthood.

As an adult with far greater autonomy, rejection is generally less of a threat to survival. And when that is the case, the peace that child worked so hard to cultivate in their outer world is now costing you the peace of your inner world. When survival is no longer the priority, authenticity is invited to step forth. And when love and compassion have a seat at the table, this is absolutely possible.

From Outer Peace to Inner Peace

Modern research continues to show that shifting our focus from earning the love of others to strengthening self-love is linked to reduced people-pleasing and improved mental health. Specifically, individuals who have actively worked on revealing their authentic self report higher levels of contentment, self-love, and confidence than those who tend toward fawning. This level of authenticity requires radical acceptance that not everyone will accept you, and that not everyone will reject you.

Source: bernardbodo / iStock

Bringing safety into the hearts of our younger selves can help with the black-and-white thinking of people-pleasing, such as: if my family or friends reject me, no one will ever want me; I’m not good enough; I’ll always be alone; etc. Since we need healthy social connection as humans to survive, when we release people-pleasing and embrace authenticity, relationships that demand inauthenticity will also be released, and those that aren’t will be stronger for it. You will be stronger for it too.

Let’s redefine what truly works in emotionally safe relationships: being loved as your authentic self, without veils, fear, or anxiety. What “worked” before was defined by the world around you not exploding. What works now will be defined by saving your inner world from eroding.
